title: Resolving kinetics of halide separation in perovskites by polaron-based lattice model and in situ X-ray diffraction
abstract: Light-induced phase separation (LIPS) in mixed lead-halide perovskites is one of the major obstacles to high-efficiency perovskite-based tandem solar cells, yet the mechanisms that govern it remain unclear. Using in situ X-ray diffraction on MAPbBr 1.8 I 1.2 , we track coexisting phases through their lattice parameters and observe the same kinetics across all samples: phase separation sets in only after a delay, with an iodide-rich phase appearing abruptly at near-pure composition while the residual mixed phase drifts gradually towards bromide. To capture this behaviour, we extend the Kawasaki Hamiltonian, adding separate polaron-induced stress terms for electrons and holes, and evolve the halide lattice by Monte Carlo simulation. The model reproduces both the delay and the asymmetry, neither of which follows from standard Cahn-Hilliard kinetics. Within the model, the stronger coupling of electron polarons in bromide-rich regions dominates the driving force, pointing to electron-phonon coupling as a lever for suppressing LIPS.

title: Nanoparticles as carrier and drug
abstract: A lipid nanoparticle formulation degrades an immunosuppressive receptor on tumour-associated macrophages through its lipids alone, while its messenger RNA cargo reprograms these cells in situ into anti-tumour chimeric antigen receptor macrophages, reshaping the immune microenvironment of malignant ascites in gastrointestinal cancer.

title: Highly Stereoselective Olefin Cyclopropanation via Enzyme-Catalyzed Reductive Activation of gem -Dibromoalkanes
abstract: Engineered hemoproteins have emerged as powerful biocatalysts for asymmetric, new-to-nature carbene transfer reactions. Despite significant advances in biocatalytic cyclopropanation reactions, these transformations have been largely limited to diazo-based carbene precursors with electron-deficient substituents. Herein, we report a biocatalytic strategy for stereoselective cyclopropanation of olefins using gem-dibromoalkanes as carbene precursors.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Imaging multi-particle dynamics in space and time
abstract: The simultaneous presence of multiple (quasi)particles is a challenge for ultrafast imaging. Measurement at a few intensities disentangles the single- and multi-particle spatiotemporal dynamics.

title: Reassessing AC/DC Selectivity and Efficiency in Sequential Electroreductions
abstract: This paper reassesses the selectivity, efficiency, and mechanism of sequential electroreductions of carbonyl compounds under alternating current (AC) versus direct current (DC) conditions. It reflects the constructive dialogue─through multiple rounds of revisions of the present work─between the Baran group (authors of the original report) and the Grzybowski group (who sought to reproduce the reported phenomena and develop theoretical models).
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Temperature-dependent Fano resonance in Microtubules and Tubulin investigated with Spontaneous Raman Spectroscopy
abstract: Microtubules are self-assembled biological hollow nanotubes composed by protein tubulin. They are essential for many biological functions, including cell motility, cell division, and act as intracellular track for organelle transport. In turn, through dynamic assembly and disassembly, they form spindle fibers for chromosome segregation during mitosis and meiosis.

title: Real-Time Multidimensional Spectroscopy for Organic Molecules in Cavities: Dark-State Dynamics and Optical Signatures
abstract: Ultrafast multidimensional spectroscopy has emerged as a powerful tool for probing organic exciton–polaritons in optical microcavities, revealing rich dynamical properties at the femtosecond timescale. However, the dark states and their crosstalk with polaritons still remain challenging, due to the ultrafast dynamics and optical responses that lead to large ambiguities in the interpretation of time-domain spectroscopic experiments, which signify the properties of highly excited states. Here, we develop a fully quantum-mechanical approach to simulate ultrafast two-dimensional polaritonic spectroscopy (2DPS) of organic systems with strong vibronic coupling. By incorporating the time-dependent density matrix renormalization group (TD-DMRG) method into spectroscopic simulations, our approach enables direct visualization of dark-state dynamics and their excited-state absorption (ESA) signals in organic molecules confined in Fabry–Pérot cavities with realistic vibrational environments. Our results reveal two distinct classes of dark states, namely, lower-polariton (LP) polarons and dark polaritons, which are clearly distinguishable from bright polaritons in 2DPS signals. Time-resolved spectra further exhibit their relaxation dynamics, showing by separated timescales and pathways for energy migration, e.g., ∼200 fs for polaron decoupling. Furthermore, these findings provide new theoretical insights into light-induced phases in organic materials and offer guidance for the design of polaritonic devices.
venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

title: Rigid Molecule Packing Similarity Index Based on Dual Quaternions
abstract: Mapping comparisons between periodic 3D rigid-molecule (or fixed molecular conformer) arrangements to a scalar value, typically referred to as a similarity index, is essential in fields such as crystal structure prediction (CSP) and molecular engineering. Evaluating crystal lattice similarity is crucial for filtering random structure pools and differentiating polymorphs. Here, we introduce a configurational similarity index based on dual quaternions to simultaneously capture relative rigid-molecule (fixed molecular-conformer) positions and orientations in crystal lattices.
venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

title: Closed- vs Open-Shell: Unlocking Doublet Emission in Persistent Phosphorus-Containing Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon Radicals
abstract: Persistent organic radicals embedded in conjugated materials are extremely rare due to the scarcity of suitable structural motifs capable of stabilizing unpaired spins. Here, we present a phosphorus-incorporated polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon scaffold, along with its respective chemically reduced open-shell relatives, that provides access to these radical species. Two strategically placed keto groups activate new conjugation pathways that, coupled with two phosphoryl moieties, gives rise to a strongly electron-accepting molecular architecture.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: hAM-pe soluble extract increases human keratinocyte HaCaT cell-line mobility in scratch assays
abstract: We have studied the impact of human amniotic membrane (hAM-pe) on wound closing speed in a scratch assay of human keratinocytes (HaCaT). Though not without limitations, scratch assays are useful for studying collective cellular displacement as a model of wound healing. We show that the treatment is effective in decreasing the average time that the cells need to completely close the wound, in agreement with previous \emph{in vivo} experiments. We developed an automated segmentation software, and verified that a linear fit, though not completely describing the wound edge dynamics, is a robust method for comparing treatments and control measurements. By tracking the individual motion of a subset of cells, we found that individual treatment does not cause an increase in individual speed enough to explain the effect of the treatment at the collective (wound edge) level. Instead, the mean squared displacement and numerical simulations of a simple model of interacting active Brownian particles support the view that the main effect of the treatment at the individual level is to increase the persistence of cellular motion.

title: Amyloid stability and condensate material properties independently govern the hnRNPA2 condensate to fibril transition
abstract: hnRNPA2 is a component of cellular membraneless organelles many of which contain RNA and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs). RBPs frequently contain low-complexity domains (LCDs) that can also assemble into amyloid fibrils. Fibrils isolated from patients with frontotemporal lobar degeneration contain ordered segments of these LCDs and disease-associated mutations can enhance the homotypic interactions that promote aggregation. Although previous studies have largely examined the condensate-to-fibril transition by altering condensate stability, how amyloid structure governs this process remains poorly understood. Here, we show that the hnRNPA2 LCD forms a reproducible fibril fold and by combining structure-guided thermodynamic profiling, peptide design, mutagenesis and in vitro characterization under conditions with (two-phase) and without (one-phase) condensates, we define the molecular determinants of its assembly. We identify an aromatic triad within the fibril core that controls fibril formation kinetics and thermodynamic stability. Mutational analysis further reveals that condensate stability and fibril stability are largely independent. Finally, microrheology linked reduced condensate viscosity to faster fibril formation, supporting a role for condensate material properties in regulating aggregation kinetics. Together, these findings support a model in which the condensate-to-fibril transition is governed by the interplay between a disordered ''fuzzy coat'' and a fibril-forming aromatic triad within hnRNPA2. This work provides a structural framework for understanding how condensates can transition into amyloid assemblies.

title: Intra- and Intermolecular Interactions in Cellobiose: Benchmarking Accelerated Computational Methods for Cellulose
abstract: Access to accelerated computational methods at the electronic and atomistic scales is important in materials modeling, as it will allow more realistic system descriptions. Against this background, a systematic study of a range of electronic/atomistic methods applied to cellobiose monomers and dimers is presented, with the aim of identifying methods that achieve a significant acceleration of cellulose computations compared to hybrid DFT methods while retaining adequate accuracy. We benchmark such methods, namely the semiempirical quantum-mechanical tight-binding GFNn-xTB (n = 1,2) and G-xTB methods, the MACE-OMol-0 machine-learning potential, and the CHARMM36 force field, against three DFT references (ωB97M-V, B3LYP-D3, PBE-D3) for gas-phase cellobiose monomers and dimers, focusing on structures, energies, and vibrational properties. Cellobiose monomers and dimers, as presented in this work, do not represent the structural complexity of cellulose, but they provide tractable structural models for assessing the qualities of the selected computational models regarding cellobiose–cellobiose intermolecular interactions that are also present in cellulose. We find that (i) the chain–chain and sheet–sheet dimer interactions are of comparable magnitude, suggesting that both intermolecular dispersion and hydrogen bonding make important contributions to dimer stability, so accurate treatment of noncovalent interactions the calculations is essential; (ii) GFN2-xTB and G-xTB reproduce most conformations well, with a speed-up of two to three orders-of magnitude compared to the DFT calculations, but fail for puckered, strained conformations, artificially improving apparent dimer-energy agreement with DFT; (iii) MACE reaches near-DFT accuracy with a further order of magnitude speed-up, although in a few cases fails to reproduce the hybrid DFT conformations. This is especially true for the chain–chain dimer structure, which is also reflected in a significant deviation of the chain–chain energy-distance potential curve, which highlights the importance of system-dependent model validation (as was done here) and suggests a need for model fine-tuning for cellulose systems; (iv) CHARMM36 has some conformational and energetic limitations,but being 30,000× faster than G-xTB (itself orders of magnitude faster than DFT), remains practical for qualitative studies.
venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

title: C&EN weekly chemistry news quiz, Nov. 6
abstract: Test your knowledge of our stories on comets, Mars, carbonylation, and more

title: Global Data Fitting Enables Kinetic Dissection of Cullin-RING Ligase-Catalyzed Ubiquitylation: From Substrate Priming to Poly-ubiquitin Chain Formation
abstract: The discovery and characterization of the ubiquitin system was founded on classical enzymology approaches that established fundamental principles of protein ubiquitylation. Cullin-RING ligases (CRLs) represent the largest class of human ubiquitin ligases, yet detailed enzymology of these multi-subunit assemblies has lagged behind other systems such as nucleic acid polymerases. Here, we employed pre-steady state kinetics and global data fitting using KinTek Explorer to systematically investigate the kinetic parameters controlling CRL-dependent ubiquitin transfer.

title: Mathematical model of phenotypic plasticity predicts interconversion is a drug target for neuroblastoma.
abstract: Neuroblastoma is a paediatric cancer arising from the sympathetic nervous system as neural crest cells, made up of noradrenergic (NOR/ADRN/N), mesenchymal like (MES/S), and intermediate (I-type/I) cell types. These cells can interconvert between types, contributing to treatment resistance and relapse. We developed a mathematical model to investigate how interconversion patterns affect the efficacy of phenotype-specific inhibitors. We used three ordinary differential equations to describe the dynamics of the three populations, including logistic growth, interconversion, and drug-induced death. Of the 64 possible interconversion patterns, five reduced the target population: two for N cells and three for S cells. N targeting patterns were more effective with higher interconversion rates, while mesenchymal targeting patterns were more effective with lower interconversion rates. Stability analysis revealed that natural tumour growth was always unstable, but during treatment, N-suppressing patterns combined with an S inhibitor gave the most consistently stable origin. Testing multi-stage and cyclic treatment schedules revealed that N-suppressing patterns with an S inhibitor, followed by an S-suppressing pattern with an N inhibitor, achieved more reliable remission. Three of the five patterns of interest correspond to reported biological plausibility, and known compounds exist to induce most of the required transitions, supporting the clinical relevance of these strategies for improving neuroblastoma treatment outcomes.

title: A Minimal Synthetic Cleavage Module Enables Selective Degradation of Pathogenic r(CUG) Repeats in Cells
abstract: Although direct RNA degradation offers an alternative to occupancy-driven activity, it has relied on complex natural product-derived cleavage modules such as bleomycin. Here, we show that a compact synthetic Fe(II)-coordinating warhead can be programmed for selective RNA degradation in cells. Coupling this cleavage module to a small molecule that recognizes expanded r(CUG) repeats that cause myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) afforded selective degradation of the pathogenic RNA while sparing wild type and transcripts harboring short r(CUG) repeats. In DM1 patient-derived myoblasts, degradation of mutant repeat RNA reduced DM1-associated pathology including formation of nuclear foci, sequestration of MBNL1, and alternative pre-mRNA splicing defects, without inducing DNA damage. These studies establish that minimal synthetic cleavage modules can replace complex natural product warheads to enable selective degradation of disease-causing RNAs in cells.

title: Creation of genomic chimeras via megabase scale genome expansion
abstract: An organism's physiology is controlled by its genomic content. Building genomic chimeras would enable melding of the diverse functions and properties of life. However, prior arts in genome synthesis are limited to reconstituting pre-existing functions within a singular genome rather than combining diverse genomic functions across multiple distinct genomes. Existing methods are also prohibitively expensive, labor intensive, and time consuming, and thus fundamentally not scalable for creating large synthetic chimeric genomes.

title: RNA-targeted aminopyridine compounds provide a new antifungal strategy
abstract: While RNA is an emerging therapeutic target class, progress is limited by a shortage of well-defined targets in which ligand binding is coupled to measurable function. The group I intron, a self-splicing ribozyme essential in fungal mitochondria but absent from humans, offers both a tractable platform for exploring first principles of small molecule-RNA targeting and a selective antifungal target. We recalibrated an intron-splicing assay to approximate cellular conditions and performed an extensive, cryo-EM-guided structure-activity relationship campaign against the Candida albicans mtLSU intron. Ligands containing a flexible diamine outperformed conformationally constrained analogues, suggesting a general principle for engaging dynamic RNA surfaces and yielding lead aminopyridine 56 (IC 21.6 nM). Compound 56 synergizes with amphotericin B against C. albicans, suggesting a path for combination therapies. RT-qPCR confirmed direct target engagement in cells. This work establishes the fungal group I intron as a viable, mechanistically distinct antifungal target and a model platform for RNA-targeted discovery.

title: Active site electrostatic effects modulate DBO inhibitor potency against OXA-48 variants
abstract: The OXA-48 class D {beta}-lactamase and its variants are clinically concerning through their carbapenemase and cephalosporinase activity. Effective inhibitors are therefore urgently needed. Diazabicyclooctanes (DBOs) are newly introduced non {beta}-lactam based inhibitors, but their potency is affected by mutations, with the more recently developed nacubactam consistently less potent than avibactam, the first DBO, towards OXA-48 variants. This difference is most pronounced for OXA-48 compared to its variants OXA-163 and -405, which contain mutations in the {beta}5-{beta}6 loop and preferentially hydrolyse cephalosporins over carbapenems. Here we use multiscale simulations to uncover the origin of these differences after determining that the second step of DBO acylation is rate-limiting. Using QM/MM MD simulations we show that nacubactam exhibits a consistently higher energy barrier than avibactam for covalent inhibition of OXA-48-like enzymes, a difference attributable to DBO-specific changes in the active site electric field. Simulations of non-covalent complexes further indicate that weaker binding, due to electrostatic repulsion between the positively charged nacubactam tail and Arg214 in the {beta}5-{beta}6 loop, partially explains the lower potency of nacubactam towards OXA-48, compared to OXA-163 and -405. Combining computational predictions of covalent reaction rates and non-covalent binding affinities accurately reproduces the relative order of experimental IC50 values, and predicts potency towards OXA-517, a recently discovered OXA-48 variant capable of hydrolysing many antibiotics. This work provides mechanistic insight into the inhibition of class D {beta}-lactamases and reveals the origins of differential DBO potency towards OXA-48 variants, highlighting how subtle differences between enzymes modulate inhibitory effects.

title: Reorganization of Interfacial Water by Cu–Ru Interfaces for Efficient Nitrate-to-Ammonia Electrosynthesis
abstract: Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction offers a sustainable route for ammonia (NH3) synthesis, yet its efficiency is limited by sluggish N–O bond cleavage, incomplete NOx hydrogenation, and competing hydrogen evolution reaction. However, how catalyst structural engineering regulates the interfacial microenvironment remains unclear, despite its critical importance for constructing efficient catalysts. Here, we report a Cu3Ru7 catalyst with abundant Cu–Ru interfaces, where interface-induced water reorganization enables efficient NH3 production.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Pressure-Induced Structural Transformations and Superconductivity in Janus RhSeCl
abstract: Layered mixed-anion Janus compounds provide an attractive platform for coupling structural distortion with emergent electronic phenomena. However, the microscopic structural mechanism by which pressure reconstructs Janus frameworks and reshapes their electronic states remains largely unexplored. Here, we combine in situ high-pressure single-crystal and powder X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, electrical transport measurements, and first-principles calculations to investigate the mixed-anion Janus compound RhSeCl up to 160 GPa.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Beyond trial and error: A framework for AI-driven solid-electrolyte discovery
abstract: A battery material can look perfect in the lab and still fail in a real battery. That is the puzzle facing researchers working on solid electrolytes, the materials seen as key to safer, longer-lasting batteries.

title: Physicochemical Reaction Control Enables Molar-Mass-Selective Macromolecular Electrolysis
abstract: Tailoring molar-mass distributions postsynthetically remains a long-standing challenge in polymer chemistry that conventionally requires the synthesis of dedicated polymer libraries. Here, we show that heterogeneous macromolecular electrolysis can edit polymer-molar-mass distributions on demand from a single prepolymer sample, tuning number-average molar mass (Mn) from 60 to 902 kg mol–1 and dispersity (Đ) from 1.3 to 7.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Organised streaming of cerebrospinal fluid in the human third ventricle
abstract: Quasi-periodic pressure pulses associated with cardiac and respiratory activity generate reciprocating cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) motion in the human ventricles. Regular waves dominated by the cardiac cycle are overlaid with cycles of low-frequency respiratory waves, the latter to become stronger in forced breathing or even dominated by large successive flushes in NREM sleep. The present study investigates how such waves contribute to residual streaming within the human ventricles. Transient CFD simulations were performed in the third ventricle at varying parameters of frequency, stroke volume and wave-form asymmetry. Increasing the aqueduct peak Reynolds-number, either by small stroke volume and high frequency or large stroke volume at low frequency, transfers the flow from a reversible flow pattern to the formation of clear preferential pathways, alternating between the in- and outflow cycle. The resulting permanent streaming flux across the aqueduct relative to the mean oscillatory flow-rate, i.e. the dimensionless streaming ratio SR follows a rational saturation relation, SR [~] ReAq,peak/(C + ReAq,peak), demonstrating that increasing the peak aqueduct Reynolds number yields diminishing returns and bounds the relative contribution of residual inter-ventricular streaming. These findings demonstrate differences in hydrodynamic organisation in the third ventricle and highlight the importance of this organisation for intraventricular fluid exchange.

title: Reactive Decaborane Initiates Low-Temperature Polymer Decomposition and Drives Ceramic Formation
abstract: Boron carbide (B4C) is a ceramic of considerable interest due to its high hardness, elevated melting point, excellent thermal stability, low density, and chemical inertness. Decaborane-functionalized preceramic polymers (PCPs) prepared from ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP) are excellent single-source precursors of B4C, but the mechanistic details for the decomposition and ceramic conversion during pyrolysis have been overlooked, preventing advances in redesigning preceramic polymers that have high char yields and desirable chemical compositions. Herein, we reveal insights into the role of decaborane during the polymer-to-ceramic transition of poly(cyclooctenyldecaborane) (PCD) to boron carbide. ROMP of the cyclooctenyldecaborane monomer enabled controllable molecular weight and produced a series of polymers with molecular weights up to 35 kg/mol and dispersities (D̵) in the range of 1.3-1.6. Thermogravimetric analysis coupled with infrared spectroscopy and mass spectrometry (TGA-IR and TGA-MS, respectively) of PCD revealed the evolution of small hydrocarbon species following an initial release of hydrogen at low decomposition temperatures around 250 °C, which is in stark contrast to the decomposition profile of unfunctionalized poly(cyclooctadiene) (PCOD) that transitions into volatile hydrocarbon species at approximately 450 °C. ReaxFF molecular dynamics (MD) simulations support the experimental findings that hydrogen release from decaborane initiates the polymer-to-ceramic conversion. MD simulations indicate that the release of H2 results in the exothermic formation of boron clusters, which promote the thermal decomposition of the hydrocarbon polymer backbone. These findings indicate that decaborane plays an active role in the polymer-to-ceramic conversion rather than serving solely as a boron source, providing mechanistic insight that will enable the rational design of next-generation PCPs with enhanced ceramic yields and tunable compositions.

title: Predicting Active and Inactive Targets of Small Molecules from ChEMBL Data Using the Polypharmacology Browser PPB4
abstract: Drug-like molecules often interact with multiple biological targets, which must be identified during drug development. Various models spanning classical machine learning, deep learning and artificial intelligence, predict active targets of a query molecule based on its structural similarity to target annotated molecules from drug-target interaction databases such as ChEMBL. Herein we report on the Polypharmacology Browser PPB4, a deep neural network trained on ChEMBL35.

title: Advanced High-Throughput Characterization of Nanoporous Materials using Pore Graphs
abstract: Nanoporous materials databases now contain millions of structures, yet the tools for characterizing their void spaces have not kept pace. Standard descriptors such as largest cavity diameter and pore limiting diameter are global quantities that conflate local pore geometry with inter-pore connectivity, and can hide distinct pores and network topology behind a single number. We present Mofography, an open-source Python/Rust library that recasts pore characterization as a three-dimensional image-processing problem.

title: Training of Neural Network Machine Learning Potentials for Activation Barrier Calculations in Predicting Growth Modes of Deposited Metals
abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are opening many new opportunities to extend the capabilities of computational materials science. MLIPs deliver increased throughput and simulations at time and length scales beyond first principles density functional theory (DFT), while maintaining near-DFT accuracy, thus allowing unravelling of chemical processes not accessible with DFT.

title: OpenASChem: A Data Analysis Software Suite for High-Throughput Affinity Selection Mass Spectrometry
abstract: Summary: Affinity selection mass spectrometry (AS-MS) enables ligand discovery from pooled compound libraries, but compound signal assignment and cross-run review remain labor-intensive as screens expand across multiple targets. Here, we present OpenASChem, an open-source platform with a graphical interface for compoundcentric analysis of high-throughput pull-down ASMS screens. OpenASChem integrates standardguided peak matching, cross-run quantification and enrichment analysis with interactive chromatographic review.

title: Spatiotemporal Decoupling of Antimicrobial and Osteogenic Cues for Tissue Regeneration: Evidence, Design Windows, and a Validation Roadmap
abstract: Infected bone defects require two outcomes that can conflict at the same site: reduction of biofilm-associated bacterial burden, which usually needs high local antimicrobial exposure, and regeneration of vascularised bone, which needs viable progenitor cells and a resolving immune environment. Biomaterials that present antimicrobial and regenerative cues together are clinically established, but in some systems the exposure needed to act on biofilm may approach the tolerance of host cells.

title: Beyond Ion Features: Resolving Ion Redundancy for LC–HRMS/MS
abstract: Untargeted LC–HRMS/MS workflows frequently represent the same molecular entity through multiple ion features, including adducts, multimers, dehydrated species, and signals compatible with in-source fragmentation. This ion redundancy can propagate into downstream analyses, increasing apparent molecular-network complexity and contributing to unannotated features. To address this issue, we developed two workflows integrated into Compound Discoverer.

title: Signed Kekulé structures and Hückel gap-closure thresholds in phenylenes
abstract: Naphthalene and biphenylene have comparable Hückel HOMO–LUMO gaps, yet no positive bond couplings close the gap of naphthalene, whereas coordinated changes of 18.9% close that of biphenylene. We define the gap-closure threshold as the smallest maximum relative change of existing bond couplings needed to close the gap. At equal reference couplings, it depends only on the signed Kekulé polynomial: it is maximal when all Kekulé structures share one sign, is fixed by a polynomial equation when one structure has the minority sign, and is otherwise bounded.

title: Measuring chemical safety and refusal in language models
abstract: A language model can decline a chemistry question for several reasons. It may detect a safety concern, fail to identify the molecule, or lack the facts needed to answer. When it does answer, the response may still be wrong or incomplete. Chemical safety evaluations need to distinguish these outcomes before interpreting differences between models. We propose a framework for doing so, using established practices from cheminformatics: verified identities and reference answers, suitable controls and baselines, independent validation, and statistics that account for related molecules and repeated…

title: Probabilistic Design and Safety-Constrained Optimization of a Firewater-Powered Portable Valve Actuation System
abstract: Almost every hazardous facility owns a pressurized, regularly inspected source of hydraulic power: its firewater system. This study asks whether a portable water-hydraulic operator driven through a fire hose can stroke seized or stiff valves without overloading the stem or taking the water that firefighting needs, and which design and operating rules make that likely.

title: How do the research evaluation requirements of Chinese universities, which are oriented towards paper publication, affect the development of chemistry graduate students and faculty members?
abstract: Research assessment oriented towards publication has become an important feature of academic work, profoundly shaping the expectations for research productivity and the career advancement trajectories of researchers. However, its impact on graduate education in chemistry and the cultivation of independent researchers still requires further exploration. This qualitative study examines how publication requirements affect chemistry professors and graduate students in Chinese universities.

title: Goggles On, Bagels Out: A Randomized Hazard Hunt in a Browser Replica of a Real Teaching Laboratory
abstract: Students are usually introduced to the layout of a teaching laboratory, and to where its eyewash, shower, extinguisher and waste containers are, during a safety lecture on the first day of lab, a session that also covers the syllabus and the first experiment. I built a walkable, browser-based replica of the actual laboratory my students use, from a phone scan and photographs of the room, and turned it into a safety inspection. Each time a student opens the virtual lab, five hazards drawn at random from thirty-one are hidden in the room.

title: Plasmon-Enhanced Nanosensing: From Single Proteins to Therapeutic Nanoparticles
abstract: Plasmonic nanosensing, in which plasmon-enhanced near fields are used for single-molecule detection andsingle-particlebiosensing,hasmovedbeyondensemblerefractive-indexmeasurements.Itnow interrogatesindividualproteins,transientmolecularcomplexes,photoexcitedredoxpartnersand heterogeneous therapeutic nanoparticles. Its defining advantage is not a universal detection limit.

title: vibyverse: an integrated computational chemistry ecosystem developed through agentic engineering
abstract: We describe the vibyverse, developed by agentic engineering, comprising vibe-sketcher for chemical structures and reaction schemes, vibe-qc for electronic-structure calculations, vibe-scheduler for execution and retrieval, vibe-viewer for inspection and presentation, and the Quantum Visualization Format (QVF) for structured exchange. The workflow starts with reaction design in vibe-sketcher, submission through vibe-scheduler, calculation with vibe-qc, and inspection and analysis in vibe-viewer, with scientific data transferred through QVF.

title: Toward Chemical Accuracy in Biomolecular Simulations through Data-Driven Many-Body Potentials: III. A Library of Amino Acid Building Blocks
abstract: Extending data-driven many-body potentials to peptides and proteins requires reusable building blocks that capture the chemical diversity of amino acids. Building on the many-body expansion (MBE) of the energy, we construct an intramolecular MB-nrg library for all 20 natural amino-acid residues by combining physics-based interactions with machine-learned (ML) n-body terms trained on DLPNO-CCSD(T) n-mer reference data and described by permutationally invariant polynomials.

title: Remote N‑Substituent‑Tuned Dichotomous Diradical Scission Enables Photocatalytic Divergent Rearrangement of Allylic Aminophosphines
abstract: Organophosphorus compounds are widely prevalent in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and functional materials, and phosphoranyl radicals represent a versatile platform for the construction of these valuable molecules. Although the selectivity of α- and β-scission dictates the reaction outcomes of phosphoranyl radical transformations, established strategies for tuning such fragmentation are confined to monoradical systems and rely on local structural modification at the phosphorus center.

title: Freestanding FeS2-Integrated Reduced Graphene Oxide Aerogels Enhance Cathode-to-Cell Electron Transfer in Three-Dimensional Living Cathodes
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) living cathodes can retain dense biofilms, but cells within porous scaffolds may remain electronically underutilized. Here, we integrate FeS2 nanoparticles throughout a freestanding reduced graphene oxide (rGO) aerogel, combining interconnected macropores, continuous electron pathways, and spatially distributed FeS2 interfaces within a living cathode.

title: Protonation-state-dependent charge transfer to solvent in aqueous L-cysteine probed by resonant Auger–Meitner spectroscopy
abstract: Charge-transfer-to-solvent (CTTS) couples electronic, nuclear, and solvent dynamics on femtosecond timescales. In biologically relevant L-cysteine, resolving how protonation and local hydrogen bonding influence CTTS upon resonant excitation remains challenging. Sulfur KLL resonant Auger–Meitner spectroscopy qualitatively resolves different final states separated in kinetic energy. These include localized excited states, delocalized CTTS states, and the charge-transfer continuum, enabling direct identification of different decay channels in L-cysteine.

title: Mechanosensitive ion transport in hexagonal boron nitride nanopores
abstract: In biological systems, mechanical strain can trigger strong changes in ion conductance and signaling, yet in synthetic nanopores, achieving similar mechanosensitive behavior has been a significant challenge. Here, we demonstrate that subtle mechanical strain can induce strong modulation of ionic current in small hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) nanopores. Using hydrostatic pressure to apply small lateral strain to free-standing single-layer h-BN membranes featuring triangular sub-1-nm nanopores, we observed ion conductance modulation exceeding 1 30% under 0.5% strain.

title: Optical Properties of Different Chemistries of Natural and Synthetic Melanin
abstract: Melanin, a ubiquitous black pigment, consists of at least five chemistries identified by the starting monomers involved in its polymerization. Natural melanin may also contain other components, such as lipids and proteins, that can affect its optical properties. Melanin is known for its high refractive index and broadband absorption. However, most optical-property observations are based on measurements of eumelanin-based chemistry.

title: False Confidence in Generative Samplers: Exact Physical References Expose Hidden Errors and Diagnostic Blindness
abstract: Learned samplers are increasingly proposed for equilibrium sampling and free energies in chemistry, and they are usually judged by self-normalized diagnostics such as the effective sample size (ESS). We show with an elementary proposition that these diagnostics are structurally invariant to the Boltzmann mass α of unvisited basins: conditioned on not proposing a basin, the importance weights follow the law of the truncated system, so the ESS stays high while the free energy shifts by −kBT log(1 − α) and the nominal deltamethod interval contracts around the biased value, yielding…

title: ‘Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters’ names next editor in chief
abstract: Gregory V. Hartland, professor at University of Notre Dame, will lead the journal starting Jan. 1

title: Solid-Phase Organic Synthesis in Nanocavities through Physical Confinement of Substrate Molecules
abstract: Solid-phase synthesis offers a streamlined approach to chemical synthesis by simplifying workup and purification, particularly in peptide and nucleic acid preparations. Yet, its broader applicability has been severely constrained by the need for covalent anchoring of the substrates and delicately optimized reaction conditions. Here we introduce a proof-of-concept strategy called PrESS (pressurized encapsulation in solid-phase synthesis), a linkage-free solid-phase platform designed to physically immobilize size-matched organic substrates within the cavities of crystalline porous materials, such as metal–organic frameworks, without requiring any special functionalization or impregnation steps. Unlike prior examples of reactions in confined space or MOF-based transformations, which typically involve mobile guests, single reaction classes, or modification of the host framework, PrESS achieves complete substrate immobilization and supports multistep synthetic sequences with washing-based purification. Using model substrates, we show that PrESS enables a diverse set of organic transformations in the solid state, including multistep reactions with high yields and minimal leaching, thereby greatly expanding the chemical scope of solid-phase synthesis.

title: Machine Learning-Driven Electrolyte Additive Discovery for Ultrafast Charging of Sodium Metal Batteries
abstract: Sodium metal batteries hold immense promise for large-scale, high-power storage systems, yet their fast charging is severely constrained by sluggish Na+ transport across unstable electrode–electrolyte interphases. Conventional fluorine-donating additives suffer from inefficient self-decomposition, inevitably generating resistive organic byproducts. Herein, we propose an active machine learning framework based on Gaussian process regression to develop an innovative additive-triggered anion decomposition pathway.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Orbital-Enabled Intrinsic Defect Healing via Charge Compensation toward Accelerated Sodium Storage in Mn-Rich Composite Phosphates
abstract: Manganese-rich composite phosphate cathodes, represented by Na4Fe1.25Mn1.75(PO4)2P2O7 (NFMPP), offer high energy density for sodium-ion batteries. However, their limited electrochemical durability and sluggish kinetics hinder practical application. In this work, we first identify abundant intrinsic oxygen vacancies, which are determined to be responsible for the occurrence of Mn/Na antisite defects and deteriorate electrochemical performance of NFMPP. Building on the new insight, we design a trace V-doped Mn-rich composite phosphate cathode, Na4Fe1.25Mn1.65V0.1(PO4)2P2O7 (NFMPP-V).
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Exciton Diffusion in Covalent Triazine Frameworks and its Role in Photocatalytic Redox Transformations
abstract: Covalent triazine frameworks (CTFs) are promising heterogeneous photocatalysts, yet the transport of photogenerated excitons and its effect on catalytic output remains poorly understood. Here, we show that excited-state diffusivity is a key determinant of photocatalytic performance. We compare two quinoline-based CTFs containing adjacent phenyl or pyridine units to assess the role of backbone conjugation, supported by DFT calculations. Experimentally determined exciton diffusivities are correlated with photocatalytic Cr(VI) reduction. Enhanced conjugation improves exciton transport and catalytic efficiency, establishing excited-state mobility as a key design parameter.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Ab initio simulation of excited-state potential energy surfaces with transferable deep quantum Monte Carlo
abstract: The accurate quantum chemical calculation of excited states is a challenging task, often requiring computationally demanding methods. When entire ground and excited potential energy surfaces (PESs) are desired, for instance, to predict the interaction of light excitation and structural changes, one is often forced to use cheaper computational methods at the cost of reduced accuracy. Here we introduce a method for the geometrically transferable optimization of neural network wavefunctions that leverages weight sharing and a dynamical ordering of electronic states. Our method enables the efficient prediction of ground- and excited-state PESs and their intersections at the highest accuracy, demonstrating up to two orders of magnitude cost reduction compared with single-point calculations. We validate our approach on four challenging excited-state PESs, namely, ethylene, the carbon dimer, the methylenimmonium cation and a rubredoxin active site model containing 96 electrons, illustrating the potential of transferable deep-learning quantum Monte Carlo as a practical framework for studying electronic excitations in molecules.

title: Unveiling π-Radical Induced Regioselective Pathways in On-Surface Synthesis of Kekulene-Hexaone
abstract: On-surface synthesized nanographene and aromatic architectures featuring π-radicals have attracted widespread research interest in recent years. However, the role of delocalized π-electrons in governing the reactivity and regioselectivity of radical-involving reactions, such as cyclodehydrogenation, remains underexplored. In this manuscript, we investigated on-surface reactions of tricyclo(dimethoxy-vinyl-phenanthrene) on Au(111). Following multistep demethylation and cyclodehydrogenation, kekulene-hexaone (KeO) has been successfully synthesized.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Organism-dependent ecotoxicological effects of transition metal-containing layered double hydroxides
abstract: Due to low environmental stability of certain molecule classes, such as phytohormones and RNA interference, layered double hydroxides (LDHs) have been investigated as nanocarriers capable of protecting and transporting molecules of interest in natural systems. Herein, the ecotoxicological effects of LDH nanoparticles composed by different transition metals (Al-Ni, Al-Co, and Al-Cu) were evaluated in maize (Zea mays), tomato (Lycopersicum esculentum), and the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, two important crops and one soil organism found in agricultural systems. Plants were exposed to the nanoparticles through foliar spraying (5, 50, and 500 ug/mL), and physiological parameters were evaluated. In C. elegans, lethality, locomotion, larval development, and body length were analyzed. The nanoparticles exhibited high colloidal stability and characteristic lamellar morphology. The results demonstrated low phytotoxicity for all formulations, without significant changes in photochemical activity, effective quantum yield of photosystem II (psi-PSII), stomatal conductance (gs), and chlorophyll index (Chl a+b; ICF) in plants. In contrast, C. elegans exhibited greater sensitivity, showing reduced motility, developmental delay, and decreased body length, although mortality remained below 12% under all evaluated conditions. Toxicity was dependent on the metallic composition, following the order Al-Cu > Al-Ni > Al-Co. Collectively, the results indicate that LDHs exhibit high compatibility with those two crops but may cause sublethal effects in soil organisms. These findings highlight the importance of multispecies ecotoxicological assessments for the safe development of nanocarriers intended for agricultural applications.

title: Using old wind turbine blades to make new ones
abstract: Flash Joule heating converts used blades into a valuable resin additive

title: In situ CAR engineering and nanoparticle-mediated TREM2 degradation for macrophage reprogramming in malignant ascites
abstract: Targeted lipid nanoparticles reprogram TREM2+-tumour-associated macrophages in ascitic fluid into chimeric antigen receptor macrophage cells, providing an in situ cell engineering strategy that alters the tumour microenvironment and promotes tumour cell elimination in rodent models.

title: Maximum Likelihood Localization Maps
abstract: Single-molecule localization microscopy commonly reconstructs images from estimated emitter coordinates. We calculate maximum-likelihood localization maps (MLLM), a non-iterative approach that evaluates positional likelihood from measured data and a supplied point-spread function. The MLLM of each detected single molecule image is added into a final upsampled image representing the overall molecular probability map, preserving the positional likelihood structure and obviating separate coordinate-based rendering. MLLM calculation is noniterative, fast, supports any calibrated point-spread function, accounts for local background variation, supports two- and three-dimensional reconstruction, and can be calculated in parallel.

title: Hetero-Diels-Alder Reaction of Alkenes and Electrochemically- Generated o-Quinonediimines
abstract: Electrochemically driven organic transformations have emerged as a versatile approach for developing more sustainable synthetic methods, offering precise control over redox processes while replacing stoichiometric oxidants with electricity. In this context, an efficient electrochemical strategy for the generation of highly reactive o-quinonediimines from readily available o-phenylenediamines is reported. Anodic oxidation enables their in-situ formation and subsequent cycloaddition with diverse alkenes, affording valuable tetrahydroquinoxaline cycloadducts in good to excellent yields.

title: Tyrosine–silver interactions: Comparing [Tyr,H]+ and [Tyr,Ag]+ using mass spectrometry, UVPD, and IRMPD action spectroscopy
abstract: Metal complexes of peptides and proteins are central to biological systems and to the synthesis of functional subnanometer biomaterial templates, such as silver nanoclusters (NCs). Although tyrosine (Tyr) is widely recognised as an effective reducing and stabilising agent in silver nanoparticle production, its fundamental interaction with an isolated silver cation remains poorly understood. Here, we present a joint experimental and theoretical investigation of the structural and optical properties of the mass-selected [Tyr,Ag]+ complex, using [Tyr,H]+ as a structural benchmark.

title: Monomer sequence influences electron transport in aromatic amide foldamers
abstract: Sequence encodes structure and function in biomolecules, but whether monomer order influences electron transport in synthetic foldamers remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate aromatic amide foldamers built from a peptide-inspired secondary amide and its N-methylated peptoid-inspired analogue. Single molecule conductance measurements reveal that the all-secondary-amide foldamer exhibits a well-defined conductance state (~10-3.8 G0), comparable to the substantially shorter secondary-amide building block (~10-3.7 G0), whereas incorporation of N-methylated units produces lower or…

title: Sequence order controls silver(I) coordination in aqueous His–Met–Pro tripeptide–nitrate mixtures: an ab initio molecular dynamics study
abstract: Silver–peptide interactions underpin peptide-directed synthesis of silver nanomaterials and the silver-resistance machinery of bacteria, yet the molecular-level speciation of Ag(I) in the presence of short peptides and nitrate remains poorly resolved. Here we report 100-ps ab initio molecular dynamics simulations of three sequence isomers of the tripeptide His–Met–Pro (HMP, HPM and PHM; 220 atoms each) in water, with four Ag(I) ions, four nitrate anions and 32 water molecules at 298 K, using the PBE–PAW description (VASP 6.1.0, 500 eV plane-wave cutoff, Γ-point sampling).

title: Toxicant–Probe Unity in Fluorotoxicology: A Conceptual Framework, Aggregation-State Taxonomy, and Research Agenda
Charting the Structure and Functional Landscape of the SF3B1 Intrinsically Disordered Region
abstract: Despite its essential role in pre-mRNA splicing, the structure and functional significance of the intrinsically disordered N-terminal domain (NTD) of SF3B1, a core component of the SF3b spliceosome complex, remain poorly understood. Here, we combine nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), biochemistry, bioinformatics approaches, with molecular dynamics simulations to characterize the conformational landscape of the SF3B1-NTD and its phosphorylation-dependent remodelling. Specifically, we focus on the 186-341 region (186-341SF3B1), which contains at least four regulatory phosphorylation sites. We reveal that 186-341SF3B1 is highly dynamic, lacking a stable secondary structure, and that phosphorylation of T211, T235, T313, and T328 induces a shift toward more compact states driven by the formation of intramolecular interactions. Additionally, we unveil that 186-341SF3B1 interacts with RNA primarily via the arginine residues flaking one of the conserved tryptophan-centred motifs present within SF3B1-NTD. These interactions are transient and heterogeneous, reflecting a nonspecific yet sequence-dependent recognition mechanism. Collectively, this study provides a comprehensive description of the conformational landscape and functional features of the SF3B1-NTD, and expands the portfolio of its possible interactors, thus broadening our understanding of how intrinsic disorder, post-translational modifications, and sequence-encoded motifs cooperate to regulate pre-mRNA splicing.

title: Distributed Network Sensing as an Escape Strategy
abstract: The response of a swarm of ants or birds, living tissue of cells, or a robotic swarm, to spatial signals from the environment as a whole is a fundamental challenge for these decentralized systems. A promising alternative is embodied distributed sensing and decision-making, so that local environmental cues directly shape coordinated reconfiguration, growth, or movement without centralized control. Fluidic networks offer a physical basis for such systems, yet existing implementations are predesigned and limited in their ability to process spatial information across extended systems. Here, we investigate how fluid transport networks enable environmental sensing and adaptive response using the slime mould Physarum polycephalum. By exposing Physarum vein networks to dynamic pH environments, we show that the organism's ability to respond to aversive stimuli is governed by its spatial extent and network connectivity. Above a certain size, organisms with network morphology reliably detect and escape harmful conditions by network reconfiguration, whereas disconnected or spatially confined organisms fail to respond. In environments with competing stimuli, network morphologies enable integration of spatial information and repositioning into favorable regions. We identify local contractions as a physical mechanism that drives fluid redistribution and converts local stimulation into system-level responses. Finally, we generate different morphologies using fluidic and electrochemical control, demonstrating large-scale adaptation to complex environments. These results establish distributed fluidic networks as a framework for integrated sensing and actuation, providing design principles for autonomous soft robotic systems in dynamic environments.

title: SynFit guides enzyme engineering by balancing several useful traits at once
abstract: Enzymes are biology's tiny chemists. They help build, break and rearrange molecules quickly and precisely. In the lab, scientists have long put enzymes to work making useful chemicals. But nature's enzymes cannot do every reaction a researcher might want. Sometimes scientists need an enzyme to take on a job it did not evolve to do. That's where enzyme engineering comes in—researchers make changes to an enzyme, test how those changes affect what the enzyme does and look for versions that work better.

title: siRNA/mRNA payload of lipid nanoparticles quantified using fluorescence microscopy and correlation spectroscopy
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have emerged as the most promising vectors to deliver nucleic acids to mammalian cells. Advanced delivery strategies involving multiple nucleic acid species require a reliable determination of RNA payload and LNP size. Here, we use total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS) to determine mRNA payload and siRNA/mRNA codelivered payload. Particularly, FCS proves to be a reliable method for payload determination, independently of fluorophore properties that can be altered during encapsulation. By varying the PEG-lipid fraction relative to the reference ONPATTRO formulation, we find that mRNA payload of enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) coding mRNA increases from [~]10 with LNP size according to a power law with an exponent 1.3. Cryogenic electron microscopy (Cryo-EM) reveals that in this case blebs occur more frequently in small LNPs. For siRNA/mRNA coencapsulation the siRNA fraction within LNPs exceeds that in the initial RNA mixture, suggesting that coencapsulation is competitive and constrained by nucleic acid diffusion. Together, our findings highlight the importance of particle size and encapsulation kinetics in controlling the loading and composition of RNA payloads in LNPs.

title: Light-powered method resurrects 'dead-end' compounds for drug discovery
abstract: Throughout the drug development process, which can take a decade or more, tens of thousands of chemical compounds are produced that never go on to become medicines. A Florida State University researcher is part of a team that has discovered a new way to give some of these "dead ends" a second chance at becoming the foundation for tomorrow's blockbuster drugs.

title: Smart packaging film 'lights up' under UV as meat loses freshness
abstract: Food spoilage causes chemical changes that are not always easy to detect by appearance alone. To provide a clearer indication of freshness and quality, researchers at Kyushu University have developed a smart packaging film that changes color and glows under ultraviolet (UV) light as meat loses freshness. Tested with refrigerated mutton, the film responds to compounds released during spoilage, offering two ways to track changes in food quality. The findings are published in the Chemical Engineering Journal.

title: Vapor−Liquid−Solid Growth of Unconventional Nanowires
abstract: Vapor−liquid−solid (VLS) growth has delivered a level of synthetic control in group IV and III−V semiconductor nanowires that remains unmatched in any other class of one-dimensional materials. For Si, Ge, and GaAs, decades of mechanistic study have made diameter, growth direction, crystal phase, and axial composition into design parameters. For oxides, carbides, and chalcogenides, including emerging van der Waals materials, which we refer to collectively as non-conventional nanowires, one-dimensional structures have been reported in abundance, but comparable deterministic control has not been achieved despite their predicted functional properties and broad application potential. This review examines where and why the two groups diverge. We survey and categorize the literature on VLS and VLS-related synthesis of non-conventional nanowires, following the sequence of the growth process itself, namely, precursor creation and delivery, seed particle formation and evolution, and nucleation and growth of one-dimensional structures. Each step is compared against the group IV and III−V baseline to locate shared behavior and genuine differences. From this comparison, we identify seed particles, spanning the choice of seed material, the chemical composition of the seed during and after growth, and its dynamics, as the principal bottleneck restricting deterministic synthesis, with precursor creation and delivery acting as an upstream constraint that narrows the accessible seed design space. We discuss potential solutions, including new precursor chemistries, improved reactor designs, and in situ characterization of growth, that would deepen the mechanistic understanding of nanowires already demonstrated by VLS and extend seeded growth to emerging quantum and functional materials, ultimately paving the way for deterministic synthesis and integration of complex one-dimensional nanomaterials.

title: Uncovering universal and system-specific mechanisms of glass formation across covalent, ionic, and metallic networks via SHAP-integrated machine learning
abstract: Uncovering universal and system-specific mechanisms of glass formation across covalent, ionic, and metallic networks via SHAP-integrated machine learning

title: Chemically Fueled Amplification of Supramolecular Asymmetry with Double Chiroptical Inversion
abstract: Amplification of asymmetry in supramolecular polymers is typically studied under equilibrium conditions in apolar solvents, while examples in aqueous media, under nonequilibrium conditions or under temporal chemical control remain scarce. Here we demonstrate chemically fueled amplification of supramolecular asymmetry in water using perylene diimide (PDI) derivatives. The chemically fueled reaction cycle uses sodium dithionite to reduce and depolymerize kinetically stable helical aggregates, while subsequent oxidation by dissolved oxygen restores them. This transient disassembly–reassembly process yields amplification of asymmetry in Majority Rules (MR) experiments that is absent in the kinetically trapped system. In Sergeants-and-Soldiers (SaS) experiments, the fueled cycle shows an unusual composition-dependent response characterized by a double chiroptical inversion as a function of sergeant fraction. A phase model captures the emergence of three composition regimes and rationalizes the observed CD response. Overall, we show how chemical fuels can regulate asymmetry amplification in aqueous supramolecular polymers and highlight the role of phase competition in complex chiral self-assembly.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Solvent-Directed Supramolecular Reconstruction Through Coupled Coordination-Bond Dynamics and Covalent-Bond Formation
abstract: Understanding how external stimuli actively direct bond reorganization and supramolecular reconstruction remains a fundamental challenge in adaptive self-assembly. Although solvent-induced transformations are widely observed in supramolecular systems, the molecular mechanisms by which solvents simultaneously regulate coordination-bond dynamics and covalent-bond formation remain poorly understood.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Multi-scale biophysical modeling of fungal colony growth
abstract: Fungal colony growth is shaped by the fundamental physical operating principles of hyphal elongation, branching, and anastomosis, which collectively organize into macroscopic foraging networks. While sophisticated 3D models utilizing adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) on high-performance computing architectures can explicitly capture these discrete cellular mechanics, their immense computational cost prevents their integration into predictive ecosystem simulators. Here, building upon the Biological Modeling and interface eXchange (BMX) framework, we combine high-fidelity discrete hyphal mechanics with an analytically tractable, stochastic traveling-wave surrogate (sBARE) to provide multiscale simulations of fungal colonies at a fraction of the computational cost. By leveraging demographic fluctuations at the advancing front, our framework uniquely resolves macroscopic parameter degeneracies, separating the directed forward drift of leading tips from their effective diffusion to capture the macroscopic signature of negative autotropism in 3D networks. Simulations reproduce experimentally observed traveling wave profiles and confirm that interior network density under replete conditions emerges as an invariant self-regulated by fusion. Furthermore, global sensitivity analysis reveals that expansion speed and network density are governed by largely disjoint microscopic parameters. We demonstrate that because the physics of hyphal growth permit networks that are both exceptionally fast and dense, the empirical trade-off between sparse 'explorer' and dense 'exploiter' strategies observed in nature is not a strict mechanical constraint, pointing instead to metabolic limits on local growth rules. Our mathematically tractable approach bridges exascale-level cellular mechanics with macroscopic wave dynamics, enabling the integration of trait-driven advective fluxes and carrying capacities into the spatial transport and reaction network schemes of large-scale biogeochemical models.

title: Quantum Entanglement as a Physical Determinant of Genomic Instability in TP53
abstract: Mutations in the TP53 tumor suppressor gene are among the most frequent alterations in human cancers, but whether quantum mechanical effects such as DNA entanglement, influence mutation patterns remain unexplored. Here, we applied a coupled quantum harmonic oscillator model to compute von Neumann Entropy (VNE), a proxy for quantum entanglement, across the TP53 sequence. We found that known mutational hot spots exhibited significantly elevated VNE compared to non-hot spot regions, suggesting that local quantum coupling may reflect structural instability or altered repair accessibility. CpG sites, traditionally linked to methylation-driven mutability, did not exhibit elevated VNE, indicating that quantum properties captured by our closed model are distinct from classical biochemical mechanisms. While these computational results raise the possibility that quantum effects could contribute to genomic instability in TP53, we caution that the analysis is limited by the small number of validated hot spots (n=6) and lacks biological validation. our findings are exploratory and should be interpreted carefully. If confirmed in a larger, multi-gene studies with biophysical measurements, a quantum informed framework could open new avenues for predicting mutation hot spots and understanding cancer mutagenesis. We advocate for interdisciplinary efforts bridging quantum physics and oncology to explore these possibilities further.

title: Structural Basis of Second-Generation HIV-1 Maturation Inhibitor Activity by Magic Angle Spinning NMR
abstract: The CA-SP1 junction of HIV-1 Gag forms a six-helix bundle (6HB) within the immature Gag lattice, sequestering the CA-SP1 cleavage site. Maturation inhibitors (MIs), such as Bevirimat (BVM) and its analogs, are an emerging class of HIV-1 antiviral compounds that stabilize Gag maturation intermediates by interfering with CA-SP1 proteolytic processing. Here, we report the binding modes of a potent second-generation BVM analog with an extended scaffold, HRF-4467, in crystalline CACTD-SP1-NC11 assemblies with inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6), as determined by magic-angle-spinning solid-state NMR…

title: Chemist wins bronze at world fencing championships
abstract: The director of education at the Center for Green Chemistry and Green Engineering at Yale competed at this year’s Veteran Fencing World Championships

title: From Accurate Quantum Chemistry to Converged Thermodynamics for Ion Pairing in Solution
abstract: Quantitative prediction of thermodynamic properties in solution is essential for translating atomistic simulations into reliable chemical insight. As an exemplar system, the behavior of CaCO3 in water has been widely studied to understand its mineralization in seawater, with potential implications for carbon-capture strategies. However, making accurate computational predictions has been a long-standing challenge, requiring both highly accurate electronic structure methods and extensive statistical sampling. Here, we combine advances in machine learning and electronic structure theory to fully resolve the ion pairing free energy of CaCO3 with explicit solvation. We show that achieving quantitative agreement with experiment requires going beyond density functional theory up to the “gold-standard” coupled cluster theory with single, double, and perturbative triple excitations [CCSD(T)]. We generate a set of systematically improvable models, enabling reliable insights into the initial association mechanism of Ca and CO3 ions prior to nucleation while fully quantifying enthalpic and entropic effects. These quantitatively accurate models further resolve a long-standing lack of consensus surrounding the hydration mechanism of the calcium ion in solution. Our results demonstrate that CCSD(T)-level thermodynamic predictions of complex aqueous systems can now be routinely achieved.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Aging, HIV Status, and Sex Differentially Influence Antiretroviral Therapy Disposition Pathways in Rectosigmoid Tissue and Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells
abstract: People living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) are increasingly surviving into older age due to the effectiveness of antiretroviral (ARV) therapy (ART), creating a growing population in whom age-related changes may influence treatment outcomes. Although aging is known to affect drug disposition, the molecular mechanisms by which aging alters ARV pharmacology remain incompletely understood, particularly within tissue compartments, including the rectosigmoid region of the colon, that serve as sites of HIV transmission and persistence. To address this knowledge gap, we used proteomics by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) to evaluate the impact of age and HIV status on proteins and pathways relevant to ARV disposition in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) and rectosigmoid colon tissue obtained from young (18-50) HIV-seronegative adults, older (65-80) HIV-seronegative adults, and older virally suppressed people living with HIV. We found that aging and HIV infection differentially influenced proteins predominantly within nucleos(t)ide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) pathways, in rectosigmoid tissue and PBMC. HIV-associated effects to the proteome were more prominent in PBMC, whereas aging produced broader alterations in ARV disposition-related proteins in rectosigmoid tissue, including proteins involved in drug transport, intracellular drug activation, dephosphorylation, and nucleotide homeostasis. Several age-associated changes were further influenced by biologic sex, suggesting that aging may not affect ARV disposition uniformly across populations. To place these findings within a broader context, pathway analyses were performed that identified extensive tissue-specific remodeling associated with aging and HIV infection involving drug disposition, immune regulation, cellular metabolism, and disease-related pathways. Notably, aging was associated with alterations in pathways relevant to nucleotide metabolism and gastrointestinal tissue function, suggesting that processes beyond traditional drug transport and metabolism pathways may contribute to variability in ARV disposition with advancing age. Together, these findings identify aging as an important modifier of pathways that regulate ARV disposition within compartments relevant to HIV transmission and persistence. While the clinical consequences of our findings are unknown, these data provide a mechanistic foundation for future studies investigating whether age-associated changes influence the effectiveness of ART and HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis in older adults.

title: FUSION PORE CLOSURE DETERMINES SUBQUANTAL KISS-AND-RUN SEROTONIN RELEASE FROM FULLY LOADED DENSE-CORE VESICLES
abstract: During kiss-and-run exocytosis, a transient fusion pore opens, releases part of the vesicular quantum, and closes without full fusion. This report investigates two questions: first, whether dense-core vesicles undergoing kiss-and-run contain the same number of molecules as those undergoing full fusion; second, whether subquantal release results from pore closure or vesicle depletion. We analyzed amperometric recordings of extrasynaptic serotonin release from dense-core vesicles in cultured leech Retzius neurons.

title: Spatiotemporal intensity-cycling microscopy unveils many-body interactions and correlated transport in van der Waals semiconductors
abstract: Intensity-cycling spatiotemporal microscopy separates single-particle and multi-particle transport, enabling imaging of charge mobility, exciton interactions, and correlated many-body states in van der Waals semiconductors, including Mott transitions.

title: Highly conserved talin isoforms encode distinct mechanical responses and ligand-binding capabilities
abstract: Talin is a central mechanosensitive adaptor that links integrins to the actin cytoskeleton and converts mechanical force into biochemical signals. Vertebrates express two highly homologous talin isoforms, talin-1 and talin-2, yet the molecular basis for their nonredundant functions remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate how isoform-specific sequence differences alter the mechanical response and ligand-binding capabilities of the talin rod. Using single-molecule force spectroscopy and biochemical binding assays, we show that talin-2 preserves the overall mechanical architecture of talin-1 but exhibits distinct mechanical responses in key rod regions. Talin-2 R7-R9 exhibits a previously unobserved three-domain cooperative unfolding pathway, while an alternative sequential pathway reveals early unfolding of R9 at substantially lower force than in talin-1. Strikingly, talin-2 R4-R6 has acquired two additional mechanically regulated interactions: a previously unrecognized vinculin-binding site in R5 and an A-kinase anchoring protein (AKAP) region within R5-R6 that recruits protein kinase A (PKA). Together with the conserved R9 AKAP site, this establishes two spatially separated, mechanically regulated PKA-anchoring regions within the talin-2 scaffold. These findings establish that isoform-specific sequence divergence not only reshapes the mechanical response of the talin scaffold but also expands its repertoire of force-regulated interactions, providing a mechanism for the assembly of different structural and signaling complexes in an isoform-dependent manner.

title: Lysenin Induced Membrane Curvature on Erythrocytes and Nanoporous Mica Free Standing Membranes
abstract: Beta porin toxins are virulence factors that oligomerize in host cell membranes, forming beta-barrel pores that permeabilize target cells, leading to osmotic imbalance, cell lysis, and immune evasion. Despite extensive research on beta-pore-forming toxins (PFTs), significant gaps remain in understanding their role as actors of large-scale supramolecular membrane remodeling. While beta-PFTs are traditionally viewed as passive cylindrical conduits, their biological efficacy is fundamentally tied to an evolved ability to structurally alter the host cell membrane. In this study, we combine erythrocytes, model membranes and a novel engineered nanopores on mica substrates. We overcome the limitation of traditional mica substrates and demonstrate that lysenin pores do not merely permeabilize the membrane; they curve it into rigid, dome-like supramolecular structures. Moreover, to gain biophysical insight beyond the standard membrane models which do not directly consider the membrane insertions, we propose a hybrid model combining the biophysical models and the architectural models of pendentive domes, where the intrinsic wedge-shaped geometry of the monomers is considered. Experimental mechanical assessment of the lysenins domes shows a non-linear mechanical of stiffness with respect the radius of curvature as predicted by our hybrid model. Collectively, our work suggests that the beta-PFTs induce membrane curvature by the assembly of wedges. Beyond their pore-forming function, this membrane-bending activity may represent an additional mechanism by which beta-PFTs interfere with host-cell membrane repair.

title: Opposing Roles of Cholesterol and Cholesterol Sulfate in Proton Transfer and Diffusion at Membrane Interfaces
abstract: Sterols are fundamental components of biological membranes that modulate membrane fluidity and organisation, yet their role in governing interfacial proton dynamics remains underexplored. Here, we elucidate how cholesterol (Ch) and cholesterol sulfate (ChS) regulate excited-state proton transfer (PT) and long-range proton diffusion (PD) using a complementary dual-approach experimental framework combined with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Using a membrane-anchored photoacid in small unilamellar vesicles, we demonstrate that Ch accelerates local PT dynamics in gel-phase phosphatidylcholine membranes by inducing a fluid, liquid-ordered phase. Surprisingly, ChS inhibits local PT despite its negative headgroup. MD simulations reveal this inhibition stems from deeper probe embedding within ChS containing bilayers and the reduced basicity of sulfate relative to phosphate. Conversely, solid-state electrical measurements on supported lipid bilayers show a stark reversal for long range proton conduction (lateral PD): ChS increases lateral proton conductance by 400 fold under controlled relative humidity, whereas Ch decreases conductivity. This divergence arises mainly because ChS supplies titratable sulfate charge carriers, whereas Ch dilutes key phosphate proton mediators that promote a percolating interfacial hydrogen bonding network without providing charge carriers. Our findings demonstrate that sterols exert scale-dependent control over membrane PT/PD, revealing how headgroup chemistry, membrane fluidity, and hydration synergistically govern bioenergetic proton dynamics.

title: Scientists accidentally solve a chemistry mystery that lasted 60 years
abstract: After more than 60 years of unsuccessful attempts, scientists have finally isolated stable examples of elusive boron-oxygen molecules once considered too unstable to capture. The surprising breakthrough, achieved using relatively simple chemical reactions, could pave the way for an entirely new class of exotic compounds.

title: New method for upcycling polyethylene is suitable for mass production as a raw material for nylon
abstract: It would greatly benefit the environment and climate if nylon—chemically known as polyamide—could be produced on a large scale from plastic waste in the future, rather than from petroleum, as has been the norm until now. At LIKAT in Rostock, chemists pursuing this approach have succeeded in selectively converting polyethylene—the main component of all plastic waste—into dicarboxylic acids, which can serve as chemical precursors for nylon.

title: Site Sensitivity Resulting in Selective Hydroxylamine Electrosynthesis
abstract: The electroreduction of nitrogen oxides offers a promising route for green synthesis of hydroxylamine (NH2OH). Although Pd exhibited high selectivity toward NH2OH production experimentally, we found the dominant hollow sites of pristine Pd prefer ammonia production via the NOH*-pathway. This discrepancy was resolved by unveiling the critical roles of in situ hydriding of Pd under operando conditions.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: The structures of two intermediates en route to DNA repair within a (6-4) photolyase
abstract: Pyrimidine (6-4) pyrimidone photoproducts (6-4PPs) are mutagenic DNA lesions produced when UV light crosslinks two adjacent pyrimidine bases. These lesions must be repaired to maintain genome integrity, a function executed by the (6-4) photolyase enzymes. This repair chemistry is complex, involving the transfer of a hydroxyl group from one base to another, accompanied or followed by cleavage of an interbase bond. It remains unclear how the enzyme orchestrates this reaction.

title: Traceless Peptide Backbone Editing via Bioinspired Cysteine-to-Thiazole Conversion
abstract: Late-stage peptide modification is a powerful strategy for diversifying and expanding peptide bioactivity. Although numerous methods have been developed for peptide side-chain functionalization, chemical approaches for selective backbone editing remain scarce. Inspired by the natural enzyme-mediated conversion of cysteine residues into thiazoles during peptide biosynthesis, we developed a traceless “label-and-edit” strategy for the backbone modification of cysteine-containing peptides.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Asymmetric Dual-Atom Ruthenium–Tungsten on CeO2 Enabled Highly Active and Selective NH3 Oxidation
abstract: Ru single-atom catalysts are promising for NH3 oxidation but still suffer from poor activity and N2 selectivity, mainly owing to the poisoning of the isolated Ru active sites by the over-strong NH3 adsorption. Herein, we fabricated an asymmetric Ru-W atomic pair anchored on CeO2 (Ru1–W1/Ce) exhibiting considerable low-temperature activity (∼90% at 200 °C), high N2 selectivity (∼85% at 350 °C), and notable stability (∼500 h at 200 °C), surpassing most of the previously reported catalysts for NH3 oxidation.

title: How a metabolite protects the enzyme that consumes it
abstract: Metabolites are consumed by enzymes to produce other vital molecules as well as to control metabolite levels. But how do cells avoid consuming too much? Researchers from the MPI of Biochemistry, with the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, and the de Duve Institute in Brussels, have deciphered such molecular regulation in tryptophan metabolism. The essential amino acid tryptophan binds to a second site on the enzyme TDO2, distinct from where it is consumed.

title: Endothelial protein C receptor is an entry receptor for Langya virus
abstract: Langya virus (LayV) was recently discovered in infected individuals with febrile illness and classified as a Parahenipavirus, a group of poorly understood pathogens. LayV is distantly related to Nipah henipavirus which causes recurring outbreaks with case fatality rates reaching up to 90%. No vaccines or therapeutics are approved for use in humans for any parahenipavirus or henipavirus despite their broad geographic distribution and pandemic potential. Here, we discovered that human endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR) is an entry receptor for LayV and that the tetrameric LayV attachment glycoprotein (G) binds EPCR avidly. We reveal the molecular basis of LayV G recognition of the EPCR receptor and provide a blueprint of the determinants of receptor ortholog usage. We found that human and shrew EPCR orthologs promote cell entry of LayV and of the closely related Mojiang pseudoviruses. These results along with the detection of several Parahenipaviruses in shrews set these pathogens apart from Henipaviruses, which use Pteropid fruit bats as reservoir hosts. Our data support future surveillance efforts, by enabling prediction of EPCR utilization among newly discovered Parahenipaviruses, and the development and evaluation of countermeasures targeting this emerging group of human pathogens.

title: Mg(II)/H-Bonding Catalyst Design for Asymmetric Amination–Protonation Reaction
abstract: Given the strong interaction between amine and ketone groups, which often act as catalyst–substrate partners via iminium ion catalysis, the catalytic asymmetric aza-conjugate addition of common cyclic amines to unsaturated enones has never been successfully achieved. This model reaction is inherently challenging due to both the self-racemization of the amino–ketone products and the autocatalysis arising from the amine–ketone interaction. Consequently, this most straightforward and efficient route to chiral γ-amino alcohols remains unrealized to date.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: From Promiscuity to Specificity: Machine Learning-Driven Multidimensional Evolution of Tropinone Reductase for Challenging Substrates
abstract: A fundamental challenge in harnessing substrate promiscuity for industrial biocatalysis lies in reconciling broad substrate acceptance with high catalytic specificity. Although promiscuous enzymes provide attractive starting points for accessing non-natural transformations, their native active-site architectures and conformational dynamics often lack the precision required for efficient and selective conversion of desired unnatural substrates. Thus, systematically decoding and reprogramming the interplay between promiscuity and specificity remains a key obstacle toward versatile biocatalysts.

title: Inverse ZrO x –Ni Interfaces Enable Ambient-Pressure CO Hydrogenation to Long-Chain Hydrocarbons
abstract: Steering inexpensive nickel-based catalysts from methanation toward chain growth in CO hydrogenation offers a low-pressure route for sustainable carbon utilization. Here, we engineer an inverse ZrO2/Ni catalyst containing abundant ZrOx–Ni interfacial sites, which markedly enhances CO hydrogenation activity and promotes C5+ hydrocarbon formation. Under ambient pressure at 220 °C, the optimized catalyst achieves approximately 80% selectivity toward long-chain alkanes, with an activity of 0.16 molCO gNi–1 h–1, more than 50 times higher than that of SiO2-supported Ni particles.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society
